clue.text: English monarch gentle here, surrounded by prize people in top seats

indicators.note: the run built from the first four words sits inside the word for prize, which wraps round it

parts.note: to bear the palm is to win the prize, so palm means prize
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword monarch
gentle means soft
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gentle English king seated among prizewinning grandees in the best seats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'surrounded by' signals the container. 'prize' is a verb-looking noun here: to bear the palm is to win. Peers sit in the House of Lords, the upper chamber of the British Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the British peerage sit in the House of Lords, the upper or top chamber of Parliament.

clue.text: Writer's about to get put inside, being a nut

indicators.note: the word for about is placed within the writer, like a prisoner put inside

explanation.surface: An author about to be jailed, as if nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get put inside' sounds like a writer going to prison, but it only signals a container.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a smooth-shelled edible kernel from a hickory tree of the American South, a kind of nut.

clue.text: Listener gets loner relaxed — one bottled up previously

indicators.note: the letter for one is kept shut inside the rearranged word, as if corked
loosened letters of loner are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A good listener meets a loner who unwinds and confides what he once kept bottled up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relaxed' rearranges the loner, and 'bottled up' keeps the one inside the result, giving LIERON.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean at an earlier time, a straight synonym.

clue.text: Finished second, then first

parts.note: top means first, as in top of the class

explanation.surface: A runner who came second and then won.
explanation.walkthrough: 'then' simply orders the pieces: S comes before TOP.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to a halt is to be done or at an end, the sense of a telegram's full stop.

clue.text: Compliment that's less exciting

explanation.surface: Praise that falls rather flat.
explanation.definitionFit: To praise someone, often insincerely, is one sense; the other is the comparative of flat, meaning duller or less lively.

clue.text: Henry wants port, but mother's denied the little beast

parts.note: Amsterdam is a Dutch port
a dam is an animal's mother

explanation.surface: Henry fancies a trip to a port but his mother says no to the small creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'denied' strikes the mother from the Dutch port, leaving AMSTER. The henry is the physics unit of inductance.
explanation.definitionFit: A small burrowing rodent kept as a pet is a little animal.

clue.text: Patio's splattered — man put round a sort of toxin

parts.note: the letters of patio plus S

explanation.surface: A patio gets splashed when a man spreads some poison round it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'splattered' makes ATPOIS, which 'put round' then encloses in the man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a poison put down to kill rodents, one type of toxin.

clue.text: It's bad having beer, designated driver admitted

indicators.note: the driver's initials are let into the beer

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: Drinking beer is bad, with a designated driver let into the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'admitted' signals the container. As an adjective the answer means rotten, as in an addled egg.
explanation.definitionFit: Used of eggs, the word means rotten or putrid, which is bad.

clue.text: Nag's home in a chaotic situation

parts.note: a nag is a horse, a mare, here possessive
a nest is a bird's home

explanation.surface: A horse's home is a scene of chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: MARES is the horse's possessive; the phrase also means an illusory discovery or a muddle.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names an untidy place or a confused, disordered state of affairs.

clue.text: My! French fashion reaches a town in Italy!

parts.note: cor! is an exclamation of surprise, like my!
ton is French for style or fashion, as in bon ton

explanation.surface: An exclamation at Parisian fashion arriving in an Italian town.
explanation.walkthrough: COR is a British exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a hill town in Tuscany, so an Italian town.

clue.text: Fighter beginning to move a bit ahead of other soldiers

indicators.note: the start of the word move gives its opening letter

parts.note: a tad is a small bit
OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: A soldier begins to advance a little ahead of the other troops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ahead of' only confirms the order. OR, other ranks, is the usual crossword term for ordinary soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: The man who fights the bull in a bullfight is this kind of fighter.

clue.text: Unsophisticated supporter falling over, grabbing something upright

indicators.note: the reversed word clutches the upright letter inside it
the supporter's word topples, so it reads backwards

parts.note: a fan supports a team
the capital I is a single upright stroke

explanation.surface: A naive fan topples while grabbing onto a post.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falling over' turns FAN into NAF; 'grabbing' takes I into it.
explanation.definitionFit: This means naive or artless, lacking worldly polish.

clue.text: Strain toes wandering around shops

indicators.note: the letters of strain and toes roam into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone strains their toes trudging around the shops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strain' and 'shops' both look like verbs; 'wandering around' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Stationers are shops selling paper, pens and office supplies.

clue.text: One nasty type grabbing another old man in the museum?

indicators.note: the first nasty type holds the next pieces within it

parts.note: a cur is a contemptible person
another nasty type, a rat

explanation.surface: A nasty character seizing another old fellow in a museum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grabbing' signals the container: the second nasty type plus old go between the U and the final letter of the first.
explanation.definitionFit: The keeper in charge of a museum's collection is the person employed there; the question mark marks a definition by example.

clue.text: A hoarder's prayer — to have gold

parts.note: a collect is a short liturgical prayer
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A miser's prayer is to own gold.
explanation.walkthrough: A collect is a brief prayer in Anglican and Catholic services.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who gathers and keeps things, stamps or coins, is a hoarder of sorts.

clue.text: Narrator full of endless jabber — would you believe his tales?

indicators.note: the storyteller contains the trimmed word inside it

indicators.note: the word for jabber loses its last letter

parts.note: to rave is to talk wildly, to jabber

explanation.surface: A storyteller who keeps babbling: can you trust his yarns?
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims the jabber word to RAV, and 'full of' puts it inside the narrator. Travellers' tales are proverbially tall stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Wayfarers are famed for exaggerated accounts of far places, hence doubtful tales.

clue.text: It's ridiculous, that's plain to see — there must be change at the outset

indicators.text: there must be change at the outset
indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for plain to see is swapped for another

parts.note: something plain to see is visible

explanation.surface: It is laughable and obvious that change must come first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there must be change at the outset' swaps the first letter V of VISIBLE; the clue does not name the new letter, which the definition supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: Laughable, deserving only derision, is the sense of ridiculous.

clue.text: Grebes in a rough stretch of water

explanation.surface: Water birds bobbing on a rough sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' rearranges GREBES IN A.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the northern arm of the Pacific between Alaska and Siberia, a body of water.

clue.text: Carriages in Australia — territory to the west

parts.note: land is territory

explanation.surface: Horse-drawn carriages in Australia heading for the western territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the west' puts LAND on the left of AUS.
explanation.definitionFit: A landau is a four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with a folding top.

clue.text: Release gang without charge

parts.note: a set is a group of people, a gang
free means costing nothing

explanation.surface: Freeing a gang without pressing charges.
explanation.definitionFit: To liberate someone is to let them go.

clue.text: Some vermin are threatening tower

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A few rats menace a tower.
explanation.definitionFit: A mosque's slender tower, from which the call to prayer is made.

clue.text: A bit of poetry mother's got hold of

parts.note: mum is a word for mother
odic means relating to odes

explanation.surface: Mother has picked up a fragment of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got hold of' signals the container; the poetry word is an adjective meaning of odes.
explanation.definitionFit: A small quantity or a little, as in a modicum of sense.

clue.text: Let's have new idea, setter! Give us a break now!

indicators.note: a new version of the letters of idea and setter

explanation.surface: A tired solver begs the setter for a fresh idea and some respite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges IDEA SETTER. The definition is a holiday season, a break from work.
explanation.definitionFit: The spring festival season brings school and bank holidays, a break from work.

clue.text: Insect given smack rolling over

parts.note: a smack of something is a taste or tang

explanation.surface: An insect hit by a swat, rolling over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smack' means flavour, not a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A small biting fly is one type of insect.

clue.text: It's taking minimal time with language
